lines.text: In Lebanon, every phone call starts with one word.
Alo.
Alo King turns that word into an order: food and essentials, ordered in a WhatsApp chat.
Lebanese families already live on WhatsApp: voice notes, Arabizi, even water and gas ordered by message.
Delivery apps ask them to download, sign up and switch, and take twenty-two to thirty percent of every restaurant order.
And most village shops only have a phone.
Alo King is WhatsApp-native. No app to download, no sign-up. Just a chat.
The customer talks, the AI understands, and our server decides prices, payments and every order state.
Customers order the way they talk: type it, send a voice note, or tap through the menu.
Arabic, English, French and Arabizi, even mixed in one message.
One smart catalogue searches every shop that delivers to them.
The basket comes back as a card, priced by our server in dollars and lira. One tap confirms it.
They pay cash on delivery, or check out with a Whish payment link.
Then they track it in the same chat, down to the driver's live location.
For the Lebanese abroad, Send Home orders for family in Lebanon and pays by card.
They can schedule it for a birthday or Eid, add a gift note, and follow it from abroad.
Behind the chat is the Alo King brain.
Taps and simple commands need no AI at all, so they are instant and nearly free. Free text uses one model call at most.
The AI never invents a price: every item, fee and time comes from our database, through typed tools.
It remembers each customer's usual order, addresses, language and stated preferences, and they can see or delete it with one tap.
Merchants get a copilot that updates availability, prices, hours and offers by text or voice, and changes nothing until the owner confirms.
And every corrected voice note makes the next one easier to understand.
Merchants don't start from zero: every shop in our pilot area is already listed, many with a draft menu.
Customers can ask them to join. The owner claims the shop with a code sent to its own phone, approves the menu, and goes live.
Orders reach every kitchen: a WhatsApp order card, a tablet portal, a kitchen printer, a phone call, or a point of sale system.
No answer in fifteen seconds? The backup fires. At forty-five, the owner's phone rings. At seventy-five, a person steps in.
And the fee is flat: one dollar per delivered meal, the first thirty days free. Not a percentage.
Delivery runs on one system with three modes: the merchant's own driver, our fleet, or a partner courier.
The dispatch brain picks the closest idle driver by road time, batches orders that fit, and checks every active order every fifteen seconds.
Drivers work from WhatsApp and a live link, with no install, and proof of delivery and cash tracking built in.
And every delivery teaches the map: landmarks, door points, and real kitchen times.
Underneath, one database is the single source of truth.
Two thousand places across Lebanon, two hundred and three Lebanese dishes with nutrition, versioned menus, and a race-tested order engine.
Every payment, fee and refund is an entry in an append-only ledger, in dollars and lira.
We earn a flat fee per order, paid promotions and sponsored placements from merchants, and a service fee on Send Home.
Our variable cost is about fifteen cents per order, WhatsApp messages and AI included.
We start in the Shouf: three hundred and fourteen merchants already listed, twelve villages, and about sixty places served.
The platform is built, and a simulator places real test orders end to end after every change.
Next, the first five merchants go live, then online payments, then growth.
Lebanon already answers with Alo. Alo King makes it an order.
